newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Grain-Rain boosts wheat crop prospects.
newsitem.headline: Australian Grain-Rain boosts wheat crop prospects.

text.p: Reasonable rainfall in Australia's parched eastern wheatbelt over the past week began to produce more bullish predictions of the 1997/98 wheat crop.
The Australian Wheat Board's (AWB) general manager merchandising Ron Storey told Reuters on Friday that a good to normal season would produce an expected crop in the 18.0-19.0 million tonne range.
Other industry figures began to look for a bigger crop than seemed likely before it began to rain a week ago.

"I would say a 20 million tonne crop after these rains is possible," Guy Allen of New South Wales grain co-operative GrainCorp Ltd said, noting that most trade estimates were still at around 18.0 million tonnes, based on the pre-rain situation. Private forecaster Australian Wheat Forecasters Pty Ltd last week raised its preliminary forecast for the 1997/98 wheat crop to 17.89 million tonnes from 17.81 million a month ago.
The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) still has the 1997/98 crop at 17.82 million tonnes.

Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders said the new crop was still seen as substantially down on last season's record 23.0 million tonnes and was likely to emerge at sub-20 million tonne figures.
"I'd put the bottom a bit lower than (the AWB)," he said.
The AWB's Storey also said that a wide variation in tonnage was possible, depending on weather.

"We expect that provided we receive good opening rains we'll have around the same acreage as last year," AWB's Storey told Reuters through a spokeswoman. "If it's a good to normal season you would expect the 18-19 million tonne range," he said.
But the absence of good to normal seasonal conditions could still reduce the crop to less than 15 million tonnes.
"It depends on weather."
Australia planted 11 million hectares to wheat in 1996/97.
Allen said rain across Australia's eastern grainbelt in the past week had been very timely and very good, with planting likely to start when the fields dried out.
"It is very encouraging," he said.
Mitchell pointed out that the large part of the eastern cropping belt still needed planting rain, although rainfall in Western Australia had been good.
The main effect of rain was confidence-boosting, he said.
Futures prices gained in nearer-term contracts last week but fell in more distant paper in a mostly weather-driven market.

Allen saw cash market prices as weaker in choppy thin trade, although they firmed slightly on Friday on U.S. futures gains. Prices fell A$10 at the beginning of the week, then recovered by A$5 on Thursday and Friday for a A$15 week's range.
Old crop wheat ended the weak at about A$188 Newcastle, while new crop was bid A$172 and sorghum was about A$165 after a steady to slightly weaker performance.
Mitchell said barley remained well bid between A$140-A$150 a tonne at farm, steady over the week but at good levels compared with a few weeks ago.
Futures broker Gary Booth of Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures said Australia still needed much follow-up rain to make the season. "It looks very dodgy at the moment," he said.
"(But) we now expect the market the market will try to move higher and may move quickly higher on a more accurate assessment of U.S. freeze damage," he said.
With the USDA crop report due on Monday, wheat markets are comfortable with some level of U.S. freeze damage but could still be surprised by the amount of damage, he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
